reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Endocrine Society clinical guidance
clinicalPearls: A 46,XY individual with an entirely female phenotype, normal or tall stature, unambiguous female external genitalia and a normally formed uterus and vagina
Bilateral streak gonads produce neither testosterone nor anti-mullerian hormone, so mullerian structures persist and no virilisation occurs
Typically presents with primary amenorrhoea and absent or arrested pubertal development in an otherwise phenotypically female adolescent

About 15 to 20 per cent of cases are caused by loss-of-function variants in the SRY gene, with other cases involving genes such as NR5A1, MAP3K1, DHH and duplications affecting the ovarian-determining pathway
Streak gonads carrying Y-chromosome material carry a substantial risk of gonadoblastoma and dysgerminoma, so gonadectomy of the dysgenetic gonads is recommended
Oestrogen and progestogen replacement is needed to induce and maintain secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone health
Because the uterus is present, pregnancy through oocyte donation and assisted reproduction is possible after hormonal preparation
reference.pathophysiology: In Swyer syndrome the karyotype is 46,XY but the bipotential gonad fails to differentiate into a testis, resulting in fibrous streak gonads. This failure of testis determination most often reflects disruption of the SRY gene or of downstream sex-determining transcription factors. Without functioning Sertoli cells there is no anti-mullerian hormone, so the mullerian ducts develop into a uterus, cervix and upper vagina; without Leydig cell testosterone the wolffian ducts regress and the external genitalia default to a female pattern. The streak gonads retain Y-derived germ cell material, which predisposes to malignant germ cell tumours, chiefly gonadoblastoma and dysgerminoma.
additionalDifferentials: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (absent uterus, testes present)
Turner syndrome and its mosaic forms
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood karyotype with SRY analysis and, where indicated, gene panel testing (NR5A1, MAP3K1, DHH)
Serum gonadotropins showing hypergonadotropic hypogonadism with low oestradiol
Pelvic ultrasound or MRI to confirm a uterus and characterise streak gonads
Tumour markers and imaging surveillance for germ cell malignancy in retained gonads
Bone mineral density assessment given oestrogen deficiency
Histological examination of removed gonadal tissue
redFlags: A palpable or radiologically enlarging gonadal mass suggesting gonadoblastoma or dysgerminoma
Signs of virilisation, which would suggest an alternative diagnosis or a hormonally active tumour
Severe osteoporosis or fragility fracture from untreated oestrogen deficiency
Delayed diagnosis leaving Y-bearing gonads in situ into adulthood
reference.prognosis: With timely gonadectomy of the dysgenetic gonads and appropriate hormone replacement, individuals have a good long-term outlook and can achieve pregnancy via oocyte donation. The main threat is malignant transformation of retained Y-bearing streak gonads, which is largely preventable with early gonadectomy.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the condition as simple delayed puberty and missing the karyotype
Leaving dysgenetic gonads with Y material in place and overlooking tumour risk
Confusing it with androgen insensitivity, in which no uterus is present
Neglecting bone protection and psychological support during hormone induction
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on disorders of sex development
management: Perform gonadectomy of the dysgenetic streak gonads to eliminate the substantial risk of gonadoblastoma and dysgerminoma from retained Y-bearing tissue
Induce puberty with oestrogen and then maintain secondary sexual characteristics with combined oestrogen and progestogen replacement, the progestogen protecting the retained uterus
Offer assisted reproduction through oocyte or embryo donation, as the uterus is present and can support pregnancy
Monitor and protect bone health with bone mineral density assessment given oestrogen deficiency
Provide psychological support and address disclosure and identity issues
Offer genetic counselling and consider testing for SRY and related gene variants
Manage through a multidisciplinary team of reproductive endocrinology, gynaecology, clinical genetics and psychology
